scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **NTA (Not the Asshole)** **Here's why, broken down clearly:** ### 1️️ **Your schoolwork is legitimate " work"** - High school online classes are **not " having the whole day off"**. Assignments, Zooms, studying, and projects require focused time and energy. Expecting a 17-18-year-old to prioritize cooking over academic responsibilities is unreasonable. - **Fact:** Schools closed *because* of a pandemic. " being home all day" doesn’t mean " free to be a full-time cook"— it means you’re juggling *both* school and home life. ### 2️️ **Your mom is shirking her responsibilities** - She finishes work at **5 PM** (earlier than your dad, who often gets home at 9-10 PM). - Yet she expects *you* and your sister to cook while **she " sits on her ass watching TV"**. - **This is a classic case of " gendered expectation"** ( " women = default homemaker" even when she’s not contributing). She’s not " being home all day"— she’s *choosing* to do nothing while demanding others serve her. ### 3️️ **Your dad is overburdened and enabling the problem** - He’s the skilled cook, but he’s working a demanding job ( often home late). - He’s *forced* to eat fast food or cook at 10 PM because **your mom refuses to learn or contribute**. - **This is not your fault**. Dad should step up and set boundaries ( e.g., " I’m exhausted from work— you need to help with dinner"). Instead, he’s taking on all the labor while your mom sits idle. ### 4️️ **Your " why don’t you cook then?" is 100% valid** - Your mom is " an awful cook" who " refuses to learn or look up recipes"— but she expects * you* to feed her? - **Logic check:** If she’s home at 5 PM and has 6 minutes to get home, she has ** ample time to throw together a simple meal** ( e.g., frozen pizza, pasta, or even microwaving leftovers). - **Her " it doesn’t take that long to cook" is hypocritical**— she’s the one who *could* do it easily but won’t. ### 5️️ **You’ve already been contributing** - You cooked during the first 3 weeks of school closure ( even baking treats like breads and cookies). - **You’re not " useless"**— you’re a high school student doing your part * within your limits*. - **Her " I’m ashamed of you" is emotional manipulation**. * She* should be ashamed of * her* lack of effort. ### ️ **The real problem here** - **Your mom is using " we’re home all day" as an excuse to avoid responsibility** while simultaneously being passive-aggressive and shaming you. - **Your dad is enabling this by always stepping in** ( e.g., " offering to cook for you" instead of demanding his wife contribute). - **You are not the problem**— you’re a kid trying to balance school and family. ### 💡 **What you should do next** - **Set boundaries:** " I have school work from 8 AM-3 PM. After that, I have 2-3 hours of homework. I can help with dinner 3 nights a week, but I can’t be the primary cook." - **Talk to your dad:** " Dad, I’m stressed about school. Mom is home at 5 PM— can you two figure out a fair system? I shouldn’t be the one cooking every night while she watches TV." - **Document everything:** If this escalates, save texts/notes about her " shame" comments. This is emotional abuse, and you deserve support. **Final verdict:** **NTA.** You’re not the asshole— your mom is. She’s using outdated, unfair expectations to exploit your time while doing nothing herself. **Your priority is school, not being her personal chef.** *(P.S. If your dad won’t step up, reach out to a trusted teacher or school counselor. This is a family dynamic that needs to change. You’re not alone.)* 💪

Okay, let me unpack this AITA scenario. The user is a high school senior asking if she's the asshole for refusing to cook dinner for her mom while schools are closed online. 

First, I need to understand the dynamics here. The key points:
- Mom works outside home (6-minute commute, finishes at 5pm)
- Dad works demanding job (home earliest 6pm, often 9-10pm)
- Dad is the skilled cook who historically does most cooking
- Mom "refuses to learn" and "complains" about cooking
- Dad often eats fast food before home because he doesn't expect dinner
- User and younger sister have online school with assignments
- User has been cooking during first 3 weeks of closure (baking etc.), but now refuses due homework load
- Mom expects "we're home all day so we should cook" but user argues school work is real work

Hmm... the real issue here isn't just about one dinner. It's about:
- Unfair distribution of household labor
- Mom's lack of participation in cooking despite being home
- Dad being overburdened
- User's legitimate academic responsibilities

* checking societal norms* 
- In most cultures, "being home all day" doesn't automatically mean free for chores - especially when school is online. School work is real work that requires focus time. 
- The fact that mom finishes work at 5pm (earlier than dad) but expects kids to cook while she watches TV... that's problematic. 
- Dad's situation is telling: he's the one who actually cooks, but he's overworked. 

* looking at power dynamics* 
- Mom's "I'm ashamed of you" reaction is emotional manipulation. 
- User's "why don't you cook then?" is valid - especially since mom is "awful cook" but still expects others to feed her. 
- Dad's pattern of eating fast food because "no dinner expected" shows this is a systemic issue, not just one incident. 

* considering the "AITA" framework* 
- AITA (Am I the Asshole) usually judges if someone's behavior is unreasonable. 
- Here, the user is:
  - A high school student with academic obligations
  - Not the primary breadwinner
  - Not the one who chose to not learn cooking ( mom did)
  - Not the one who's been consistently shirking responsibilities ( mom has)

* red flags in the scenario* 
- Mom's "s sitting on her ass watching TV while expecting others to serve her" - that's not " being home all day" it's " being home all day and doing nothing productive"
- Dad's " forced to make dinner at 10pm after work" - that's not sustainable
- User's " I try to help if no homework" - shows she's willing to contribute, but has limits

* societal context* 
- In many households, " women = default cook" is a harmful expectation. But here, mom is *choosing* not to cook while expecting others to. 
- The " we're home all day" argument is being used to exploit the kids' time. School work is real work - it's not " having the whole day off" as the user correctly points out. 

* personal judgment* 
- User is absolutely not the asshole. 
- The real assholes here are:
  - Mom for being passive-aggressive, not contributing, and using " shame" as a tool
  - Dad for not setting boundaries (though he's overworked, he's enabling the dynamic by always stepping in)
- But the question is specifically about the user's action today: Refusing to cook when she has school work. 

* why user is right* 
- 1. School work is her primary responsibility right now ( high school senior, college applications etc.)
- 2. Mom has no right to expect her to be a full-time cook while mom watches TV
- 3. " It doesn't take that long to cook" is false - meal prep takes time, and mom's " low effort flavourless meals" show she's not even trying to make it efficient
- 4. Dad is the one who should be cooking ( he's home first, he's skilled, he's the one who's been doing it) but he's overburdened

* the " AITA" verdict* 
- NTA (Not the Asshole) 
- In fact, the user is being reasonable. 
- The real problem is the entire family's dynamic where mom shirk responsibilities and dad enables it. 

* what the user should do* 
- Not just " refuse to cook" but set clear boundaries: " I have school work from 8am-3pm, then I have 2 hours for homework. I can help with dinner 3 nights a week if needed, but I can't be the primary cook." 
- Dad needs to step up - he's the only one with authority to change this. 
- Mom's " I'm ashamed" is emotional manipulation - she's the one who's not contributing, not the kids. 

* final thought* 
- This is a classic " gendered expectation" problem where mom is treated as " the homemaker" but isn't doing homemaker work. 
- User is 17-18 years old - her job is school, not being a full-time cook for her family. 
- The fact that she's been helping with baking etc. shows she's willing to contribute, but mom's " we're home all day" is a false premise. 

* verdict* 
- NTA. User is not the asshole. The real issue is the family's unbalanced labor distribution and mom's lack of participation.
